title: Add the decodeTimedOut arm to the app's image-decode copy (ipass-f8p consumer break)
description:
PassesCore's public DecodeFailureReason gains .decodeTimedOut on the ipass-f8p stack. The enum is non-frozen but SPM builds without library evolution, so switches must be exhaustive.

CONFIRMED BREAK: imageDecodeErrorCopy at ios-main/Packages/Feature/Sources/Passes/scannable/CreateScannableCardScreen.swift:472-483 switches all five reasons with no default. The app depends on the kernel by LOCAL PATH (../../passes-ios/passes-ios-main), not a version pin, so it breaks the moment the stack lands on main - there is no window to sequence around.

Also CreateScannableCardImageImportTests.copyDistinctAcrossAllArms iterates DecodeFailureReason.allCases and asserts copy is distinct and non-empty, so the new arm needs its own wording, not a reuse of decoderUnavailable's.

Copy should follow the ADR rationale: a timeout is a load signal the same input may survive, so it says retry - distinct from decoderUnavailable's 'couldn't scan that image just now'. FrameScanLoop.handle matches bare .decodeFailed and needs no change.

title: withDecodeTimeout reports false timeouts under cooperative-pool saturation (REPRODUCED)
description:
On the macos-15 runner the barcode decode timeout did not bound the caller's wait
anywhere near its budget. decodeTimeout is a documented security control (the
slow-loris guard, ADR barcode-decode-1) whose docblock claims it "bounds the
wait", so this is worth understanding rather than writing off as CI flake.
Surfaced while investigating ipass-42i. NOT FIXED - documentation only.

ESTABLISHED FACTS.
 1. Run 30921911346 (sha 09051f9): slowOperationYieldsTimeoutValuePromptly
    measured elapsed 7.30s against a .milliseconds(100) budget - a ~70x overshoot.
 2. Rerunning the IDENTICAL sha produced a different failure set: 8
    PassesBarcodeTests Vision decode tests returning
    DecodeFailureReason.decoderUnavailable, plus the same timing test. 10 total.
 3. decoderUnavailable is returned BOTH for a Vision perform failure
    (VisionSymbolDecode.swift:25) AND as the timeout value
    (BarcodeFrameDecoder.swift:65, BarcodeImageDecoder.swift:53). So (2) is
    consistent with timeouts firing rather than Vision being unavailable, but the
    reason code cannot distinguish the two - which is itself a gap.
 4. In that run EVERY test reported 8-10s elapsed, including trivial store tests,
    so the whole runner was slow, not just this path.

WHAT DID NOT REPRODUCE (so do not assume the mechanism).
An earlier hypothesis - that Task.detached parks a cooperative-pool thread with
the synchronous blocking operation and starves the deadline's Task.sleep
continuation - was tested and NOT confirmed. Probe: 24 concurrent
withDecodeTimeout calls, each blocking 3s via Thread.sleep, 100ms budget, 8 cores.
Worst observed elapsed 0.107s; every deadline fired on time. The full suite also
passes 3/3 locally, and 12 spinning busy-loops did not reproduce it either.
So pool exhaustion alone does not explain it on Apple silicon; the mechanism
remains UNKNOWN.

PLAUSIBLE REMAINING EXPLANATIONS, none verified:
 - 3 vCPUs on the hosted runner versus 8+ locally may cross a threshold the probe
   could not reach. Worth re-running the probe with the pool capped to 1-2 threads.
 - General runner slowness (fact 4) may mean the budget is simply too tight for
   that hardware, in which case the test is measuring the environment.
 - Something specific to the runner's Vision/Metal stack blocking differently than
   Thread.sleep does.

WHY IT MAY MATTER TO USERS, if the mechanism turns out to be real: a slow or busy
device could report decoderUnavailable for a legitimate scan, and the guard would
fail to bound the wait exactly when load makes that guarantee valuable.

NEXT STEPS.
 - Reproduce deterministically before changing any code. Cap the cooperative pool
   (e.g. LIBDISPATCH_COOPERATIVE_POOL_STRICT) or run the probe on a 3-core VM.
 - Compare against PassesCore's SignatureVerifier.runBlocking, which documents this
   exact class of hazard and keeps blocking work off the cooperative pool using a
   dedicated Thread / DispatchQueueTaskExecutor. It is the in-repo precedent if a
   fix is warranted, but confirm the mechanism first.
 - Consider splitting decoderUnavailable into a distinct decodeTimedOut reason so a
   hung decoder is distinguishable from a slow one. Public enum change
   (BarcodeDecodeResult.swift), so it needs its own decision.
notes: Fix complete and verified: PR #55 (stacked on #54). 4 consecutive green full-ci runs. Awaiting human merge - not closing until merged.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
REPRODUCED DETERMINISTICALLY (2026-08-04). Mechanism confirmed; it is a genuine defect in withDecodeTimeout, NOT a runner artifact.

DECISIVE CI EVIDENCE (run 30922880530, on main, AFTER the @MainActor fix; 608 tests, 13 issues):
  'Test fastOperationReturnsItsResult() recorded an issue at DecodeTimeoutTests.swift:13:9:
   Expectation failed: (result -> "TIMED_OUT") == "REAL"'
That test is withDecodeTimeout(.seconds(5)) { "REAL" } - a closure that returns a string
literal. It cannot take 5 seconds. No amount of runner slowness explains it. Note also that
slowOperationYieldsTimeoutValuePromptly PASSED in this run, so the two tests fail in
alternation: the race resolves both ways.
The other 12 issues were HostilePayloadFidelityTests decodes returning != .decodedBarcode -
i.e. the same false timeout on the real Vision path.

LOCAL REPRO, 100% deterministic (not flaky): probe replicating DecodeTimeout.swift verbatim.
Saturate the Swift cooperative pool with sustained work, then run an instant operation
against a 5s budget:
  saturation    tasks   trials  TIMED_OUT   worst
  none          -           12       0/12      0ms
  cpu-bound     8           12      12/12   5332ms
  parked        8           12      12/12   5331ms
  both          32          12      12/12   5332ms
8 saturating tasks on 8 cores is enough. 100%, not intermittent.

GROUND TRUTH: instrumented so operation() stamps its own completion time. Under saturation
the stamp is NEVER set - operation() never runs at all. So the timeout does not fire because
the decode was slow; it fires because the decode never got scheduled.

ROOT CAUSE. Everything in withDecodeTimeout except the deadline lives on the shared Swift
cooperative pool:
  - operationTask is Task.detached -> queued on the cooperative pool, starvable indefinitely.
  - both watcher Task {} closures -> also on the cooperative pool.
  - the deadline is Task.sleep -> a TIMER, which fires on wall-clock regardless of pool state.
So when the pool is saturated the deadline ALWAYS wins, and the operation may not have
started. Two failure modes, one root cause:
  (1) deadline beats work that never started -> false decoderUnavailable (fastOperation +
      the 12 HostilePayloadFidelity failures).
  (2) the caller's continuation resume is itself queued on the saturated pool -> the 7.30s
      overshoot on a 100ms budget (slowOperation, run 30921911346).

WHAT SATURATES THE POOL ON CI: swift-testing runs all 608 tests in parallel (no .serialized
traits anywhere in Tests/). On a 3-vCPU runner the pool is 3 threads wide. PassesCoreTests
signature tests park pool threads via SignatureVerifier.runBlocking's semaphore.wait(), and
PassesBarcodeTests run concurrent synchronous Vision decodes. runBlocking's own comment
already names this exact hazard: 'parallel callers can park every pool thread at once with
nothing left to make progress.'

CORRECTS FACT 4 IN THE DESCRIPTION: 'every test reported 8-10s' is NOT evidence of a slow
runner. swift-testing reports per-test wall-clock while tests run concurrently, so every
test's elapsed spans the whole run window. Local baseline shows the identical pattern (17
tests all reporting 0.116-0.19s against a 0.215s suite total). The CI run window was 11.782s
total for 608 tests - that is a FAST run, not a slow one.

WHY THE EARLIER HYPOTHESIS DID NOT REPRODUCE: the old probe used Thread.sleep, which the
kernel workqueue sees as a blocked thread and compensates for by adding threads. Sustained
work that never yields the pool is what starves it. Also re-tested and refuted: 96 concurrent
CPU-bound ops on 8 cores (worst 107ms) and LIBDISPATCH_COOPERATIVE_POOL_STRICT=1 (no effect).
Concurrency alone is not the trigger; sustained pool occupancy is.

USER-VISIBLE IMPACT (real, not hypothetical): on a busy device a legitimate scan returns
decodeFailed(.decoderUnavailable) because the decode never got a thread. The guard mislabels
load as a broken decoder, exactly when the device is under load. The docblock claim that it
bounds the wait for 'a slow or hung Vision decode' does not hold as written.

FIX DIRECTION (unimplemented, needs §7 sign-off): move the operation off the cooperative pool
onto an executor the module owns - the in-repo precedent is SignatureVerifier's
DispatchQueueTaskExecutor - and resolve both arms without depending on cooperative-pool
scheduling. Note a partial fix is not enough: moving only the operation still leaves the
watcher tasks on the pool.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
CANDIDATE FIX DID NOT WORK - recording the negative result so it is not retried blindly.

Tried the obvious shape: run operation() on a module-owned concurrent DispatchQueue and the
deadline on a separate serial DispatchQueue via asyncAfter, so neither arm sits on the Swift
cooperative pool. Under the same probe saturation it still returned 12/12 false timeouts
(worst 5333ms cpu-bound, 5492ms parked). It DOES still time out genuinely slow work correctly
(3s op / 100ms budget -> 8/8 TIMED_OUT at 108ms), so the fix is not simply inert.

Two candidate reasons, neither yet separated:
 - The probe's saturators are too blunt. 32 never-yielding spinners drive the machine to 100%
   CPU, which starves ANY implementation - that is CPU exhaustion, not pool blocking, and no
   scheduling fix can beat it. The CI mechanism is more likely pool BLOCKING (threads parked
   on semaphore.wait with no thread-add) than CPU exhaustion, because {"REAL"} needs only
   microseconds of CPU and a merely-busy machine would still time-slice it in under 5s.
 - The cooperative pool and libdispatch global queues share one pthread workqueue with
   per-QoS thread limits, so 32 parked userInitiated threads may starve the dispatch queues
   too. If so, moving off the cooperative pool is necessary but not sufficient.

Also still unaddressed by that shape: withCheckedContinuation resumes the CALLER back onto
the cooperative pool, so a blocked pool still delays observation of the result even when the
right value was chosen.

CONCLUSION ON METHOD: stop tuning a synthetic local saturator - it over-fits. CI reproduces
this 100% (every full-ci run red since 2026-07-27, and the fastOperation failure is
unambiguous), so CI is the correct reproduction environment. Next attempt should push a
branch and cycle the full-ci label to measure against the real 3-vCPU runner rather than
against a hand-built local approximation.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
FIXED AND VERIFIED ON THE REAL RUNNER. PR #55 (stacked on #54).

FIX: withDecodeTimeout submits decodes to a bank of dedicated serial DispatchQueues the module
owns, and puts the deadline on its own owned lane. Start latency of a trivial block, pool parked
and CPU idle:
  Task.detached (old)         1.7ms free   >20000ms parked
  concurrent DispatchQueue    0.4ms free   >20000ms parked
  DispatchQueue.global        0.0ms free   >20000ms parked
  dedicated SERIAL queue      0.0ms free       0.1ms parked
  dedicated Thread            0.2ms free       0.1ms parked
Concurrent and global queues draw from the same thread pool the cooperative pool exhausts, so
only dedicated lanes are immune. This is why the earlier concurrent-queue candidate failed and
why SignatureVerifier's serial DispatchQueueTaskExecutor was the right precedent all along.

TWO SIZING LESSONS, both found on the runner and not locally:
 1. Lane width must track IN-FLIGHT DECODES, not cores. Vision runs the decode out of process,
    so a lane waits on that service rather than burning a core. Width = activeProcessorCount put
    41 concurrent decode tests ~14 deep on 3 lanes and blew the 5s budget by queueing alone.
    Now 16.
 2. Widening lanes does NOT rescue the fidelity suites. ~41 concurrent Vision decodes on a
    3-core runner genuinely exceed 5s because Vision's out-of-process service contends for the
    same three cores - the guard reporting a real overrun, in suites that are not testing it.
    Those suites now pass a generous budget; the timeout keeps its own coverage.

REGRESSION TEST: decodeRunsOnAnOwnedLaneNotTheCooperativePool asserts the lane label. Against
main it fails with 'ran on com.apple.root.user-initiated-qos.cooperative'. It inspects the lane
rather than parking the pool for real: the behavioural version works but starves sibling suites
including FieldLinkScanner's sub-500ms assertions - manufacturing this bug's own blast radius
inside the suite guarding against it is not a good trade.

TEST-BOUND CHANGE, called out for review: slowOperationYieldsTimeoutValuePromptly keeps the exact
security assertion (had the caller waited on the operation, the result would read REAL) and
demotes the wall-clock check from <1s to a <10s backstop. This is NOT loosening the security
property. How soon the CALLER is released depends on the caller's own executor, which this guard
does not control and which the loaded runner delayed to 5.26s. The race itself is decided
off-pool, so the deadline beats the operation regardless of pool state - which is what the value
assertion pins.

RESIDUAL, documented in the ADR: this fixes which executor the decode runs on, not that resuming
the caller needs the caller's own executor. A caller with a blocked pool still observes the result
late. The guard bounds the wait it controls; it cannot bound delivery into a blocked caller.

ADR barcode-decode-1 updated with a dated entry. DecodeFailureReason.decodeTimedOut added.
full-ci: 3/3 consecutive green on macos-15 (30946939310, 30947150792, 30947443593) against a
prior history of zero successful runs ever.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
ROUND-TWO REVIEW: a bounded lane bank was not enough, and my green claim was wrong.

The review flagged a new compiler warning (var lane captured in a concurrent closure,
#SendableClosureCaptures, the only warning in the package). Real - and correctly noted that my
'both linters clean' claim was true of the linters but not the compiler, which I had not checked.
Package.swift is swift-tools-version 6.0, so these targets are in Swift 6 language mode where
that diagnostic is on track to become an error.

Chasing it surfaced the bigger problem. Re-verifying on CI produced a FAILURE at the previous
tip de73a58 (run 30991764987): fastOperationReturnsItsResult returned TIMED_OUT against a 5s
budget - the original symptom. So the earlier '5 consecutive green runs' recorded on this bead
was luck. Measured rate was about one failure in three. Correcting that here so the record is not
misleading.

ROOT CAUSE OF THE RESIDUAL FLAKE: a bounded lane bank reproduces the defect at a higher
threshold. ~44 concurrent decodes on a 3-core runner keep all 16 lanes occupied, so an instant
operation queues and reports decodeTimedOut without ever starting. Least-loaded selection
narrowed the window but could not close it. Documenting the residual was not sufficient - it was
still a live defect, just rarer.

FIX: a free lane is reused; when every lane is occupied the work spills to a transient thread
rather than queueing. The invariant is now absolute - a decode never waits behind another decode,
so only its own duration can exhaust its budget. Occupied lanes are the normal case rather than a
corner, because a timed-out decode is orphaned but keeps running (Vision perform is
non-cancellable). Spilling is bounded by concurrent demand, which the app controls; untrusted
input cannot inflate it, so thread count is not attacker-reachable.

LESSON WORTH KEEPING: for this guard, any bounded executor turns a burst into a false timeout.
The only safe invariant is that a decode never queues behind another decode. If a future change
reintroduces a queue (a pool cap, a semaphore, a serial fallback), it reintroduces this bug.

TEST: decodeDoesNotQueueBehindSaturatedLanes - 24 concurrent holders against 16 lanes, then an
instant decode on a 500ms budget. Verified to discriminate: with spill 24/24 holders start and
the decode returns REAL; without it only 16 start and it returns TIMED_OUT. The settle wait is
bounded on purpose - the first version HUNG on regression instead of failing, which is worse than
no test.

VERIFIED: 613 tests, 6/6 local runs, warning-free from-scratch build, both linters clean, and 6
consecutive green full-ci runs on a3fbcc7 against a measured ~1-in-3 failure rate on the commit
it replaces.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
ROUND THREE: the spill I added in round two was an unbounded thread source, and my security claim about it was wrong.

WRONG CLAIM, CORRECTED. I wrote (in this bead, the commit, and the ADR) that spill thread growth
was 'bounded by concurrent demand, which the app controls; untrusted input cannot inflate it, so
thread count is not attacker-reachable.' That is false. Orphaned decodes never release, because
Vision perform is non-cancellable, so in-flight count is CUMULATIVE rather than concurrent. An
image crafted to wedge Vision is untrusted input and is exactly the slow-loris case this guard
exists for; re-fed by the per-frame scan loop (which has no back-pressure in the kernel) it mints
a permanent thread per frame. Unbounded thread growth ends in a crash, which is worse than the
degraded decode the spill was protecting.

FIX: cap the spill at 64 threads; past the ceiling decodes queue again, spread across lanes.
Measured: 300 submissions produce exactly 80 concurrent (16 lanes + 64 overflow) and 74 new
threads, remaining 220 queued. overflowThreadsAreCapped pins it.

STANDING TENSION, worth remembering before anyone 'fixes' either side:
 - Queueing a decode causes FALSE TIMEOUTS (round two).
 - Never queueing causes UNBOUNDED THREADS under a wedged decoder (round three).
Both are real. The resolution is: never queue up to a ceiling, then queue. Anyone removing the
ceiling reintroduces the crash; anyone lowering it toward zero reintroduces false timeouts.

ALSO FIXED THIS ROUND:
 - QoS inversion: spilled decodes ran at .default (raw -1) while lanes ran at .userInitiated
   (raw 25), verified by direct measurement. Spilling happens when pressure is highest, so the
   decode most needing its budget was scheduled below the others, and .default throttles first
   under Low Power Mode / thermal pressure.
 - The saturation test discarded its precondition (started-holder count), so it could pass
   without ever exercising the spill path - most likely on the loaded runner it guards.
 - ADR cited decodeRunsOnAnOwnedLaneNotTheCooperativePool, renamed on this branch.
 - stackSize = 512*1024 was a measured no-op (platform default for secondary threads is exactly
   524288). Removed. Overflow threads are now named for thread dumps.
 - The context assertion was weak on the spill path: a bare Thread reports the fallback label
   com.apple.root.default-qos.overcommit, evidence of nothing. Now asserts positively against the
   lane prefix or the overflow thread name.

TEST-ISOLATION FINDING: the two new tests failed TOGETHER in the full suite while passing in
isolation - the ceiling test consumes the whole overflow budget, starving the saturation test's
spill. They contend for one process-global bank. The DecodeTimeout suite is now .serialized and
the ceiling test drains fully before yielding. Any future test that saturates the bank must
account for this.

VERIFIED: 614 tests, 6/6 local runs, warning-free from-scratch build, both linters clean, 6
consecutive green full-ci runs on 8bbf0ab.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
ROUND FOUR: lane accounting leaked past the ceiling, and my own test was flaky.

DEFECT (reviewer point 1, confirmed and worse than described). The past-ceiling queued branch
dispatched with no completion closure, so a lane's busy flag stayed owned by the decode already
running there. That decode clears the flag on completion WHILE the queued decode is still
executing on the same serial lane, so the lane reads free and the next submit queues behind
untracked work. Measured: after the ceiling engaged once and the original holders retired, 16 of
16 fresh decodes timed out with lanes idle. With depth counting: 0 of 16. Total failure of the
guard in that state, and it outlives the pressure that caused it - so it escapes the 'only past
the ceiling' condition it was documented under.

FIX: busy [Bool] -> depth [Int]; free is firstIndex(of: 0); every dispatch increments and every
completion decrements, queued branch included.

ALSO: the ceiling test asserted concurrent < 300, which passes for any ceiling up to 299. A cap
raised to 200 would have gone undetected by the test whose job is pinning it.

MY OWN FLAKY TEST - the lesson worth keeping. Tightening those assertions made them fail 4 of 12
CI runs on CORRECT code. Two causes, both mine:
 1. awaitSignals polled with a BLOCKING semaphore wait, holding one of the runner's three
    cooperative-pool threads while waiting for tasks that needed that same pool to start. The
    harness was starving what it measured. Invisible on 8 cores.
 2. Even fixed, '80 saturators must start within 20s' is an assertion about the RUNNER, not the
    guard. On 3 cores it is not reliably true.

RESOLUTION: stop brute-forcing. The accounting is pure logic, so it is now a value type
(LanePlacement) that DecodeLanes holds under its existing lock. Invariants pinned at two lanes
and a ceiling of one, deterministically, in microseconds. Verified both replacements
discriminate: reintroducing the untracked-queue bug fails 5 assertions, raising the ceiling fails
11. Barcode suite went 4.6s -> 1.6s.

GENERAL LESSON: for this module, integration tests that saturate the real 16-lane bank are how
bugs get FOUND but are the wrong thing to GUARD them with - the preconditions are statements
about the runner. Prefer LanePlacement unit tests for accounting invariants; keep exactly one
cheap end-to-end check for the wiring. Shipping a flaky test to guard against flakiness is the
trap here, and I fell into it once.

VERIFIED: 618 tests, 6/6 local runs, warning-free build, both linters clean, 8 consecutive green
full-ci runs on 3f4ed1d.

title: full-ci (macOS) has been red on main since 2026-07-27
description:
The macOS build/test workflow (.github/workflows/full-ci.yml) has failed on every
run since 2026-07-27; no run has ever succeeded. Because ci.yml is lint-only and
the `full-ci` label did not exist in the repo until 2026-08-04, nothing surfaced
it: the Monday cron sweep failed silently.

CAUSE 1 (fixed on branch cms-wire-order, commit 09051f9): two main-actor
isolation compile errors in Tests/PassesUITests/CompactCodeViewTests.swift.
CompactCodeView is a SwiftUI View so its static renderImage is @MainActor;
validPayloadsRenderThroughTheKernelEncoder and
encodeFailuresRouteToFailureTileNotPlaceholder called it from a synchronous
nonisolated context. Introduced with 7352345 (ipass-dq2). Local `swift test`
does NOT reproduce (Swift 6.2.4, arm64-apple-macosx26.0) - needs the macos-15
runner.

CAUSE 2 (open): DecodeTimeoutTests.slowOperationYieldsTimeoutValuePromptly is
timing-fragile on a loaded 3-core runner. It asserts elapsed < 1s for a 100ms
budget while the operation does Thread.sleep(forTimeInterval: 3) - a blocking
sleep occupying a cooperative-pool thread, so the timeout task may not be
scheduled for seconds. Observed elapsed 7.3s. In that run EVERY test reported
8-10s elapsed, indicating global saturation rather than a specific regression.
Passes 3/3 locally.

FOLLOW-UPS:
 - Decide whether to make the test robust (run the blocking op off the
   cooperative pool, or assert against the budget with a generous multiplier)
   rather than loosening the security-relevant property that a hung decode stops
   blocking the caller.
 - Consider making full-ci a required check once green, or alerting on the cron
   failure, so a red macOS gate cannot go unnoticed for a week again.
notes: Gate is green (4 consecutive full-ci runs). Alerting in PR #54, root-cause fix in PR #55. Required-check follow-up split to ipass-szw. Awaiting human merge.

comments.author: Cole Bittel
comments.text:
GATE IS GREEN. Root cause was ipass-f8p, not the environment.

CORRECTION TO CAUSE 3 IN THE NOTES: 'Vision is not reliably available on the macos-15 runner'
was wrong, and so was the conclusion that a green macOS signal is unobtainable. Vision works
fine on the runner. Every one of those decoderUnavailable failures was withDecodeTimeout
reporting a false timeout - the value was ambiguous because the enum conflated the two. The
run-to-run variation that read as an unstable environment was the race resolving differently
each time, not Vision appearing and disappearing.

CORRECTION TO CAUSE 2: 'the whole runner was slow, every test reported 8-10s' is also wrong.
swift-testing reports per-test wall-clock while tests run concurrently, so every test's elapsed
spans the whole run window. That run was 11.782s for 608 tests, which is FAST. Local runs show
the identical pattern.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG, in the order it had to be fixed:
 1. @MainActor compile errors - already fixed on main (25a2c61).
 2. withDecodeTimeout scheduling decodes on the cooperative pool - ipass-f8p, PR #55.
 3. FieldLinkScanner ReDoS guards measuring wall clock - ipass-sry, PR #54. Pre-existing and
    independent; flaked ~50% locally under the parallel suite and would have kept the gate red
    on its own.
 4. Fidelity suites coupled to the 5s production budget, which ~41 concurrent Vision decodes
    genuinely exceed on 3 cores. Fixed in PR #55.

Nothing was serialized or skipped to get here, and no test was rearranged to manufacture a
green result.

ALERTING (PR #54): a Linux job scoped to github.event_name == 'schedule' opens, or comments on,
a standing ci-sweep-failure issue when the cron sweep fails. Scoped to schedule deliberately -
push and label runs already surface their own red state. This is the specific hole that let main
sit broken from 2026-07-27: the cron had no PR to turn red.

REQUIRED CHECK: not done, and deliberately left for a human decision. It needs a branch-
protection change, and it should only go in after the gate has a track record - the run history
is 5 consecutive greens against a prior history of zero successes ever. Filed as its own issue.

Also corrected the workflow header's cost note: the 10x macOS multiplier applies to PRIVATE
repos. This repo is public, so full-ci bills nothing - confirmed via the Actions timing API
(MACOS: 0s billable on every run). That is why iterating against the real runner was the right
method here rather than tuning a synthetic local saturator.

title: Accept signedAttrs signed in wire order (walt-ios ios-wbn.3; Android wpass-x70)
description:
Mirror of walt-passes-android 824abc5 / wpass-x70 (user-reported, GH walt-app/walt-passes-android#176). Consumer tracking bead: walt-ios ios-wbn.3.

CONFIRMED EMPIRICALLY 2026-08-04, not assumed. Repro: detached CMS blob with signedAttrs SET elements reversed out of DER order, signed over exactly those bytes; sorted control through identical machinery. Control -> ok(appleVerified). Wire order -> failed(signatureCryptoFailure). Repro method: surgery on a CMS.sign envelope - reorder the [0] signedAttrs children, re-sign the SET-tagged encoding with the leaf key, rebuild via order-preserving DER.Serializer.serialize(_: ASN1Node).

TWO INDEPENDENT LIBRARY BEHAVIOURS:
 1. swift-asn1 DER.lazySet (DER.swift:187) THROWS 'SET OF fields are not lexicographically ordered'. CMSSignerInfo's BER init deliberately routes signedAttrs through DER.set ('SignedAttrs MUST be in DER'), so an unsorted set fails at PARSE.
 2. CMSSignerInfo._signedAttrsBytes() re-serializes via serializeSetOf, which sorts - the same re-encode-before-hash BouncyCastle did. Moot, (1) fires first.
Consequence: iOS reports Tampered(SignatureCryptoFailure) where Android reported Tampered(ManifestSignatureMismatch). Same user-visible rejection of a sound pass, different arm - tests mirroring Android's assertion must expect the iOS arm.

NO DEPENDENCY-BUMP ESCAPE: pinned swift-certificates 1.19.1 / swift-asn1 1.7.0; newest upstream tag 1.19.2 is doc-only.

SCOPE EXCEEDS ANDROID'S. Android's fallback replaces only the signature-math leg; BouncyCastle still supplies chain classification. Here the library bails at parse and supplies nothing, so the fallback must also drive the chain:
 a. hand-parse the blob (DER.parse does NOT apply the set-order check) -> sole SignerInfo, wire-order signedAttrs bytes re-tagged as SET, sole messageDigest value, digest + signature algorithms, signature OCTET STRING, embedded certificates;
 b. digest(manifestBytes) == messageDigest, constant-time;
 c. Certificate.PublicKey.isValidSignature(rawBytes, for:signatureAlgorithm:) over the wire bytes under the leaf key;
 d. chain: Verifier(rootCertificates:policy:).validate(leaf:intermediates:), then the same appleVerified / selfSigned / certChainIncomplete mapping classify() uses.
FEASIBLE: every piece is PUBLIC API of the pinned deps (verified against sources). Byte-level CMS surgery precedent exists in CMSSignatureAlgorithmNormalizer.swift.

PORT ANDROID'S REVIEW HARDENING: fold every fallback error to false so the fallback can only confirm the strict path's rejection, never relabel it; read both halves of the binding from ONE parse; require exactly one messageDigest attribute carrying exactly one OCTET STRING; fail closed on absent attributes, multi-signer envelopes, indefinite-length BER. Pin both directions in tests plus a control asserting the stock library still rejects the fixture, so the regression tests cannot go vacuous.

SECTION 7: security architecture and a deviation from the Android pattern. Needs human sign-off before implementation - and the approval is heavier than ios-wbn.3 originally described, because it now covers a hand-rolled CHAIN leg as well as a hand-rolled verification leg.
notes:
SECTION 7 SIGN-OFF GRANTED 2026-08-04 (user). Approach approved: "as little
Walt-authored security code as possible" - Option A, STRIP-AND-DELEGATE. This
SUPERSEDES scope items (a)-(d) in the description, which planned a full
hand-parse including a hand-rolled chain leg.

APPROVED DESIGN. swift-certificates parses SignerInfo.signedAttrs as OPTIONAL
(CMSSignerInfo.swift, DER.optionalImplicitlyTagged tagNumber: 0), and when it is
absent CMSOperations.swift:415 verifies the signature directly over `dataBytes`.
The fallback exploits that legitimate path:
 1. DER.parse the ORIGINAL blob (no SET-order check applies) -> sole SignerInfo.
 2. Lift the [0] signedAttrs node, re-tag as SET, serialize order-preserving via
    DER.Serializer.serialize(_: ASN1Node). These are the bytes the issuer signed.
 3. From that SAME node, read the sole messageDigest attribute value, and require
    constantTimeEqual(digest(manifestBytes, signer.digestAlgorithm), it). This is
    the ONE check the library can no longer perform, and it is load-bearing: the
    library never validates contentType, only messageDigest.
 4. Rebuild the blob with the [0] signedAttrs element REMOVED.
 5. CMS.isValidSignature(dataBytes: wireAttrBytes, signatureBytes: strippedBlob,
    ...) with the same anchors/intermediates/PermissivePolicy, mapped through the
    EXISTING classify() switch, unchanged.
The library therefore still owns signer-certificate location, the
digestAlgorithmFor(signatureAlgorithm) == digestAlgorithm cross-check, the
signature math under the leaf key, and the full Verifier chain build. No second
copy of the appleVerified / selfSigned / certChainIncomplete mapping exists.

RISK THE HUMAN ACCEPTED: the design uses a spec-legitimate library behaviour in
an unintended way. Mitigation required in the implementation: a test pinning the
"signedAttrs absent -> verify over dataBytes" behaviour directly, so a future
swift-certificates release that tightened it fails loudly rather than silently.

RULED OUT DURING INVESTIGATION, do not revisit without new information:
 - Reusing the library's parsed structures. CMSContentInfo / CMSSignedData /
   CMSSignerInfo are `internal`, NOT @_spi(CMS) public. Unreachable.
 - Letting the library classify the chain on the unmodified blob.
   CMS.isValidSignature checks the signature BEFORE the chain
   (CMSOperations.swift:415 then :427), so a blob whose signature it rejects
   never reaches chain validation. Some hand-rolled leg is unavoidable.
 - Sorting signedAttrs into DER order and re-verifying. The signature is over the
   unsorted bytes, so this reproduces the failure.

title: Cap the decode lane queue and refuse past it, rather than retaining images unboundedly
description:
Past the 80-thread ceiling, LanePlacement.claim() falls through to depth[lane] += 1 with no cap (Sources/PassesBarcode/DecodeTimeout.swift). Each queued submission retains its payload behind a lane head a wedged decode never releases: a CGImage up to the ~50MP BoundedImageDecode limit (~200MB RGBA), or a camera CVPixelBuffer (~8MB at 1080p BGRA, 30/s from the frame loop). The far end is a jetsam kill.

Found independently by both a security review and a branch review of PR #55.

NOT A REGRESSION - before the lane bank the same closures queued unboundedly on the cooperative pool and retained the same buffers. This is a pre-existing hole the ceiling work made visible, which is why it did not block PR #55.

PROPOSED FIX: give LanePlacement a total in-flight cap and a third Target case (.refused). submit() drops the work; the already-scheduled deadline resolves the caller with its timeoutValue, so the bounded-wait property is unchanged and nothing is retained. spillsOnlyUntilTheCeiling would then assert refusal rather than .lane(0).

WEIGH BEFORE IMPLEMENTING: refusing means the caller waits the full budget for an answer that was decided instantly, and legitimate burst load would turn into failures rather than slow successes. Reaching the cap needs 80 cumulative wedged decodes, so the trigger is genuinely pathological.
acceptance_criteria: Queue depth is bounded; a submission past the cap retains nothing; the caller still observes a bounded wait; LanePlacementTests pins refusal.

Review of the ipass-f8p-ci-green branch found one real flake risk and three doc/accuracy defects.

1. DecodeTimeoutTests.decodeDoesNotQueueBehindSaturatedLanes still requires all 24 holders to start within 20s - the last runner-dependent assertion on a branch whose purpose was removing them. The precondition it actually needs is every lane claimed plus one spill, which is decodeLaneCount + 1 signals, since claim() fills lanes before spilling and a signal implies a claim.
2. The .serialized docblock justifies itself by naming the ceiling test, which this branch moved to LanePlacementTests and which no longer touches real lanes. The trait is still correct but its stated reason is gone.

configuration rather than splitting them.

ONE THING THE REVIEW MISSED. Its fix for point 1 changed only the comparison, leaving the poll bound
at "upTo: hogs". awaitSignals polls until it has upTo signals or the deadline expires, so the test
would have kept waiting the full 20s for the 7 holders it no longer needs, then passed. The bound
had to move with the assertion.

WHY THE RELAXATION IS SOUND. claim() takes depth.firstIndex(of: 0) before considering overflow, so
lanes fill before anything spills, and a signal implies a claim. decodeLaneCount + 1 signals
therefore proves all 16 lanes are at depth >= 1 plus one spill - exactly the precondition the final

full-ci is now green and stable (5 consecutive successful runs on macos-15 against a prior history of zero successes ever - see ipass-42i, ipass-f8p). The remaining half of 'a red gate cannot go unnoticed' is making it block merges rather than just report.

A required check that never runs on unlabeled PRs would block every PR indefinitely. Enabling this therefore also needs the trigger widened to pull_request: [opened, synchronize, reopened], which changes it from a safety net into a per-PR gate on every push. That is a real cost/latency tradeoff (~2-3 min per run, though runs are free while the repo is public) and is the actual decision to make here, not the branch-protection toggle itself.

RATIONALE: making full-ci required requires widening its trigger to pull_request [opened, synchronize, reopened] AND relaxing the job's 'if:' guard (github.event.label.name == 'full-ci'), since a skipped required check blocks a merge permanently. That turns a safety net into a per-PR gate on every push: measured 2m05s-3m23s per run on macos-15, paid on every push to every PR. Runs bill nothing while the repo is public, so the cost is latency and workflow friction, not money. Judged not worth it at current team size.

The mitigations are the 'full-ci' label on risky PRs, the push-to-main run, the Monday cron sweep, and the alert job (ipass-42i / ipass-h2t).

REVISIT IF: the repo goes private (the 10x macOS multiplier starts billing and the tradeoff shifts further against), or an unlabeled PR lands a break on main that the label model should have caught.

title: FieldLinkScanner ReDoS guards measure wall-clock, flake under the parallel suite
description:
phoneScanCompletesQuicklyOnPathologicalInput and mixedAlphaDigitSoupCompletesQuickly assert wall-clock elapsed < 500ms. Under the full 610-test parallel suite they fail roughly half the time on an 8-core machine (observed 508ms, 513ms, 533ms, 546ms), and they will be worse on the 3-vCPU macos-15 runner. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING: reproduces on main at adaca77, independent of the ipass-f8p work.

These are catastrophic-backtracking guards. The property they defend is that scan() does not blow up exponentially on pathological input - a real regression would be seconds or unbounded, not 533ms. Wall clock measures the machine's contention, not the algorithm.

FIX: measure thread CPU time (clock_gettime(CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID)) instead of wall clock. FieldLinkScanner.scan is a synchronous pure function so thread CPU time captures all of its work, and it is immune to scheduler contention while still catching real blowup.

Blocks a green full-ci gate (ipass-42i).

title: normalizeCMSSignatureAlgorithm: map SHA-1 -> sha1WithRSAEncryption (walt-ios ios-k7u)
description:
Found while investigating ipass-10g / walt-ios ios-wbn.3. Consumer tracking bead: walt-ios ios-k7u.

CMSSignatureAlgorithmNormalizer.combinedRSA(forDigest:) covers sha256/384/512 only. A pkpass whose SignerInfo carries digestAlgorithm=SHA-1 with the bare rsaEncryption signatureAlgorithm OID - the wire shape Apple PassKit ships, and the shape of the real pass reported in GH walt-app/walt-passes-android#176 - is left unrewritten. swift-certificates does not know bare rsaEncryption, so AlgorithmIdentifier(digestAlgorithmFor:) throws and the pass reads Tampered.

swift-certificates DOES support .sha1WithRSAEncryption (SignatureAlgorithm.swift; Signature.swift:369 verifies via Insecure.SHA1), so the fix is one more arm in combinedRSA(forDigest:) plus the sha1 digest OID constant (1.3.14.3.2.26).

Keep this separate from ipass-10g: with it, the strict CMS path keeps owning SHA-1 passes and the ipass-10g wire-order fallback stays scoped to the ordering problem instead of silently becoming the SHA-1 path too.

Needs a SHA-1 + bare-rsaEncryption fixture; the existing apple-signed fixture is SHA-256.
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST REAL PASSES 2026-08-04 (review follow-up, commit 5d27084).
Two real SHA-1 pkpasses on hand (pass-file-samples ticket(4).pkpass, TechBBQ) both
verify ok(appleVerified) through the fix, and read failed(signatureCryptoFailure)
with the SHA-1 arm removed. Both encode digestAlgorithm as SEQUENCE { sha1, NULL }
at the SignedData and SignerInfo levels.

SECOND ENCODING ALSO NOW HANDLED. SEQUENCE { sha1 } (parameters absent, how Apple
encodes SHA-256) is legal DER and was left reading Tampered, because
AlgorithmIdentifier(digestAlgorithmFor:) maps .sha1WithRSAEncryption to .sha1
(NULL) while every other digest maps to a ...UsingNil variant, and the check is ==
on a synthesized Hashable. Fixed in 5d27084; requires rewriting the SignedData
digestAlgorithms SET together with the SignerInfo, since CMS.isValidSignature also
checks digestAlgorithms.contains(signer.digestAlgorithm).

NO ANDROID PARITY COVER: BouncyCastle's DefaultCMSSignatureAlgorithmNameGenerator
resolves from OIDs alone and never reads getParameters() (verified by javap,
bcpkix-jdk18on 1.84), so absent-parameters SHA-1 verified on Android while failing
on iOS. The fix closes that divergence.

title: Threat-model + ADR amendments for redesigned list surfaces
description: Analogue of Android wpass-tjc.4 (walt-passes-android PR #187, ADR/threat-model amendments). The consumer redesign changes what kernel-rendered untrusted content appears WHERE: actual barcode renders and PDF page-0 thumbnails now appear on wallet LIST card faces (previously detail-only), a compact code-render path exists whose output is explicitly not scannability-guaranteed (the list-face concession), and the consumer detail surface composes kernel BarcodeView inside a consumer-built card rather than kernel PassFront (trust captions become consumer-owned text). Amend the kernel threat model + ADRs to record: (1) list-face rendering of untrusted content still flows exclusively through the kernel's bounded decode paths (BoundedImage-equivalent guards, isolated PDF rasterization) - enumerate the invariants a consumer must uphold; (2) the compact-render concession and why quiet-zone/white-backing are still enforced at small sizes; (3) the trust-presentation boundary: which trust signals the kernel guarantees non-suppressibly (ExpiredOverlay inside PassFront, ScannableCardScreen provenance caption) vs which the consumer now owns when composing primitives directly, and what the consumer contract is (mirror the language Android PR #187 settled on). Read walt-passes-android's merged amendments first and port the reasoning, not just the text - flag any iOS-specific divergence (e.g. no isolated-process renderer on iOS; Data Protection instead) explicitly. Docs-only bead; no code.
close_reason: Merged via PR #43 (squash): ADR passes-ui-6 ports wpass-tjc.4 reasoning (issuer color pkpass-only, content-true previews on existing bounded paths, no verified affordance at list scale) and makes the kernel/consumer trust-presentation boundary explicit for consumers composing BarcodeView directly. security-review: no findings. cole-branch-review: Merge.

title: PDF pager support: thumbnail cache capacity + adjacent-page prefetch
description: Analogue of Android wpass-tjc.3 (walt-passes-android PR #186, pager adjacent-page prefetch). The redesigned consumer document detail is a horizontal pager with a symmetric next/previous-page peek (~56pt insets) and an n/N pill; each page is a kernel-rasterized thumbnail. Android found the kernel cache default too small for the peek window: with beyondViewportPageCount=1 the pager can hold up to ~5 live page bitmaps plus prefetch, and evicting a still-painted bitmap crashes - they exposed cache capacity (consumer passes maxSize 7) and added adjacent-page prefetch. AUDIT the iOS kernel's PassesPDFUI surface (PDFThumbnail.swift: PDFThumbnailState, PageImageHandle, PDFThumbnailCache, PDFThumbnailViewModel.start/stop, ThumbnailRenderTarget/Context) against those needs: (1) is PDFThumbnailCache capacity configurable by the consumer? (2) can the consumer warm/prefetch adjacent pages without visible jank when swiping? (3) are handles safe against eviction-while-displayed (iOS may already be safe if PageImageHandle retains its CGImage - verify and document)? Implement whatever is missing, mirroring the Android PR #186 API shape where it fits Swift. If the audit finds iOS already safe and sufficient, close this bead with the audit written up in the close reason and an ADR note - a no-op outcome is acceptable.
close_reason: Audit complete, no kernel change needed - landed as ADR passes-pdf-ui-6 via PR #42 (squash). (1) PDFThumbnailCache(maxSize:) already public, consumer passes 7. (2) Eviction cannot invalidate a displayed page: no-op onEvict + strong CGImage-backed PageImageHandle; Android's recycle crash class structurally absent under ARC. (3) Peek prefetch works through existing public PDFThumbnailViewModel + shared lock-guarded cache; no speculative API added. security-review: no findings. cole-branch-review: Merge.

title: Isolate the still-image and live-frame decode lane banks
description:
DecodeLanes.shared is one process-global bank serving both VisionBarcodeImageDecoder (untrusted files, via share sheet / PHPicker) and VisionBarcodeFrameDecoder (app-owned camera pixels). Orphaned decodes never release their slot, so occupancy is cumulative for the process lifetime.

CONSEQUENCE: ~80 wedging still-image imports, one at a time and with no concurrency needed, permanently pin the whole bank. From then on the live camera scanner returns .decodeTimedOut for every frame until the app is force-quit, and nothing in the module can observe or report that state.

Raised by the PR #55 security review. Not a merge blocker: it needs a pathological input repeated ~80 times, and the pre-change implementation shared the cooperative pool between the two paths just as broadly.

OPTIONS: separate banks per decoder so a wedge on the untrusted path cannot starve the trusted one; and/or track cumulative orphan count and surface a distinct saturation reason so the consumer can tell 'timed out' from 'the decoder is exhausted and will not recover'.
acceptance_criteria: A wedged still-image decode cannot reduce live-frame decode capacity; ADR barcode-decode-1 updated.

title: iOS decodeTimedOut has no Android counterpart - decide whether to mirror
description:
The iOS kernel now has DecodeFailureReason.decodeTimedOut; passes-android's enum has five arms and
folds the timeout into DecoderUnavailable, whose docstring reads "could not be bound or terminated
before returning a result".

That divergence is defensible: Android's ProcessKiller kills the isolated decode, so a timeout there
really is an unavailable decoder, whereas iOS cannot kill Vision mid-decode and must distinguish a
slow decoder from an absent one. Conflating them already cost a misdiagnosis on iOS (ipass-42i).

But README says the iOS kernel mirrors passes-android, and the app-side copy test was named "every
DecodeFailureReason arm maps to its Android wording". Both are now qualified in comments rather than
resolved. Decide whether Android should gain the arm too, or whether the mirror claim should be
scoped to say the failure taxonomies intentionally differ where the process models do.

title: full-ci alert job misses cancelled cron sweeps and its own failures (ipass-42i follow-up)
description:
Raised in the second review of the ipass-f8p stack. Belongs to full-ci.yml, which is PR #54's
change (branch ipass-42i-cron-alert), so it was not folded into the ipass-air commit - filing
rather than tangling a third branch into the stack.

1. The alert job guards on failure(), which is false for a cancelled run. The pre-existing
   concurrency group keys on github.ref, so a push to main while the Monday cron sweep is running
   cancels the sweep and the sweep never alerts. Partly mitigated because the cancelling push run
   alerts on its own failure, but it covers a different commit.
2. If the alert step itself fails, the degradation is uneven: a failing "gh issue list" lookup only
   loses dedup, but a failing "gh issue create" reddens a job nobody watches - which is the exact
   failure mode the job was added to prevent.

Worth deciding whether the alert should also fire on cancelled(), and whether a create failure
should escalate somewhere a human sees.
notes:
PARTIALLY ADDRESSED by the ipass-air commit, which landed in #55 (9ffaff8) rather than #54. Point 2's lookup half is done: 'gh issue list' now degrades with '|| echo ""' so a lookup blip loses dedup instead of reddening the job under set -e. The alert also now fires on push to main, not just schedule.

STILL OPEN: point 1 (failure() is false for a cancelled run, so a push that cancels the Monday sweep leaves the sweep silent) and point 2's other half (a failing 'gh issue create' still reddens a job nobody watches, with nowhere to escalate).
